notes.meaning: The bride wishes her beloved were like a brother to her. Then she could kiss him even out in the street, and no one would think badly of her. Christians have long read this as the church longing to be close to Jesus all the time. Christ has become like our Brother, so wherever we meet him we should gladly show our love and not fear being laughed at.

differ.view: Read this mainly as a couple's love. In her culture, husbands and wives did not usually show affection in public, but a brother and sister could.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars call verses 1-2 a 'lover's wish song', like ancient Egyptian love songs. In such songs the wish is exaggerated on purpose.

notes.meaning: She would bring him home to her mother's house. There he would teach her, and she would give him her best spiced wine. In the traditional reading, the mother's house is the church, where Christ teaches his people. The 'spiced wine' is our love and service. These please Jesus, who gave us everything first.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some read the verse plainly as a bride offering herself to her husband in married love, in private at home.

notes.meaning: These words repeat what she said in chapter 2:6. She pictures his arms around her and holding her up. Read as a picture of Christ, his power holds us up so we do not faint in hard times. His love comforts us.

For the third time she gives this charge to the 'daughters of Jerusalem', her friends. In the traditional reading, the church warns her children not to do anything that would grieve Christ and make him seem far away. When we are tempted, we should ask ourselves, 'Why would I push away the One I love?'

differ.view: See it as a warning not to rush love or stir up passion before the right time. Love is sacred and should not be played with.

notes.meaning: Onlookers admire the bride as she comes up from the wilderness, leaning on her beloved. Christians have seen here a picture of a believer coming out of a life of sin, which is like a dry, lonely desert. We come out leaning on Christ by faith, not on our own strength or goodness. In the second half, Christ reminds her how he raised her up when she was dead in sin, under the shade of the tree she once compared him to.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars read the apple tree as the place near her family home where their love first began. On this reading, the couple is now visiting it.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The old Latin Bible (the Vulgate) says her mother was 'corrupted' under the tree. Some old readings took the tree to be the Cross, or linked the verse to Eve's sin and the promise of mercy.

notes.meaning: She asks him to keep her close, like a seal worn on his heart and arm. A seal was a precious stamp that was never let go. Christians see Christ as the High Priest who carries his people's names on his heart, with his love and his power both pledged to them. Love is as strong as death. Its 'jealousy' is a burning devotion that will not share the beloved with anything else. Christ's love for us was stronger than death itself.

differ.view: Read the seal as a picture of married love: lasting, belonging and secure, a poetic 'until death do us part'.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: 'The fiercest blaze' is literally 'flame of Yah', the only place God's name appears in the book. Many scholars think it is simply a way of saying 'the greatest flame of all'.

notes.meaning: No flood of trouble can put out true love, and no fortune can buy it. Christ's love for us was not drowned by the worst suffering. In the same way, a believer's love for him cannot be scared away by hardship. Nor can it be bought off with all the world offers. Nothing but Christ himself can satisfy the heart that loves him.

differ.view: Apply it to marriage: 'Sex can be bought; love must be given.' Real love is priceless.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Douay-Rheims Bible translates it 'many waters cannot quench charity', using the old word for love.

notes.meaning: The speakers have a little sister who is not yet grown. They ask how they can help her when someone seeks her hand. In the traditional reading, the Jewish church is caring for the Gentiles, people who are not Jewish and did not yet have God's word. It can also mean anyone not yet brought to Christ. Those who know Christ should think about how to help others come to him.

differ.view: Read it plainly as her brothers, long ago, planning for the day their young sister would be asked to marry.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars feel the poem really reaches its peak at verse 7. Some think verses 8-14 were added later.

notes.meaning: If she is a wall, they will build silver towers on her. If she is a door, they will protect her with cedar boards. Traditionally, this is Christ's answer about the little sister. If she builds on him like a firm wall, he will keep building her into a fine palace. If she is like a door, he will guard her so no harm comes. Small beginnings of grace, God's kindness at work in us, will grow.

differ.view: See a wall as a girl who stays pure and a door as one open to temptation. The family will either honour her or guard her closely.

notes.meaning: The bride says she is a strong wall, grown up and secure. She has found favour, or 'peace', in his eyes. In the traditional reading, she thanks God that his grace made her strong. She trusts him to do the same for her little sister. We should look back with joy on the times God showed us his favour.

differ.view: Read it as a woman who guarded her honour when young. Because of that, she now has peace in her marriage.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The word 'peace' (shalom) may be a play on the name Solomon. It shows she found true peace with him.

notes.meaning: Solomon rented his vineyard to workers, who each paid a thousand silver coins. The bride says her own vineyard is hers to give. Traditionally, the vineyard is Christ's church, which he trusts us to care for, and he looks for fruit. Our hearts are our own vineyards to guard. The best fruit, the thousand, belongs to Christ. Those who work for him, the two hundred, are well rewarded too.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many read 'my vineyard' as the bride herself. Unlike Solomon's rented vineyard, she is not for sale; she gives her love freely.

notes.meaning: He speaks to her as one who lives in the gardens and asks to hear her voice. In the traditional reading, Christ speaks to his church in her many gatherings. While he is away, he wants to hear her prayers and praises often. He is not bothered by our prayers; he delights in them.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some read it simply as Solomon asking his bride to sing for her old friends in her home country, as she used to.

notes.meaning: The Song ends with her calling her beloved to hurry, swift as a gazelle on the mountains of spices. Christians have long heard this as the church praying for Christ's return: 'Come, Lord Jesus.' Heaven is pictured as those sweet mountains, where he is now. The book ends with longing, reminding us to wait eagerly for him.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some read it as a happy close to a love song. The couple go off together over the fragrant hills.
